claims.text: A WVTaTiCr refractory high-entropy-alloy coating can be deposited by laser cladding.
Laser-clad WVTaTiCr coatings significantly improve the corrosion resistance of stainless steel.
42-CrMo steel is an example of a stainless-steel substrate.
The relevant coating uses WVTaTiCr with the full Cr level, corresponding to Cr x = 1 in the cited series.
Full Cr inclusion induces Laves-phase precipitation.
A 3.5 wt% NaCl solution is a relevant corrosion-test environment for the laser-clad WVTaTiCr coating.
The relevant NaCl exposure occurs at room or moderately elevated temperature.
Laser cladding with the specified coating produces grain refinement.
Laser cladding with full Cr produces a Cr2Ta Laves phase.
The Cr2Ta Laves phase enhances passive-film stability.
Optimized Cr content increases lattice distortion.
Increased Cr content drives controlled Cr2Ta Laves-phase precipitation during laser cladding.
The Laves phase forms a network within a refined dendritic structure.
The refined, Laves-containing structure promotes formation of a compact passive film.
A compact passive film limits ion diffusion and thereby reduces corrosion attack.
The coated steel will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than uncoated steel.
Improved performance will be evidenced by lower corrosion potentials.
The coating will slow mass loss relative to uncoated steel.
Corrosion enhancement may depend on coating thickness, laser-cladding parameters, temperature, and corrosive-medium composition.

contradictions.description: The substrate is framed as stainless steel while 42-CrMo steel is given as the example and is the substrate in the cited record; the hypothesis does not establish that this alloy is stainless steel.

The mechanism predicts enhanced passivation, but the outcome identifies a lower corrosion potential as evidence of improvement. Corrosion potential alone is not a corrosion-rate metric, and a shift to lower potential does not by itself demonstrate improved passivation.
